title: A cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 8–9)
hookLine: the Macedonians gave out of poverty; God loves a cheerful giver
tomorrow: what do you say when someone claims you got it all secondhand?

lines: THE FIRST ONE TO CHIP IN.
cards: A fundraiser link drops in the group chat, and the first person to chip in is the one who just lost shifts at work. It happens. Paul saw it happen.
The churches of Macedonia, he tells Corinth, were in "a great trial of affliction" and "deep poverty," and they gave anyway, to a collection for poor believers far away.
More than they could afford, he says, and nobody had to ask them twice. How?

teach.b: Paul's answer is joy: "the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality." Joy plus poverty added up to generosity.
They "first gave their own selves to the Lord," and the money followed.

teach.h: BY WHAT YOU HAVE, NOT WHAT YOU DON'T.
teach.b: And he won't set a price: "If there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not."
Then the heart of it: "Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." Now a neighbor.
Muslims keep sayings of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the hadith collections.

teach.h: A SMILE IS CHARITY: THE HADITH.
teach.b: One says that your smile in your brother's face is charity. Another says every kind act is charity. Shared ground: a gift is weighed by the heart, not the size, and even a face can give.
The honest difference: Islam also has zakat, a required giving that is one of the pillars of the faith, alongside the free giving called sadaqa.
Paul's collection is free will, "not of necessity," though some Christians keep a set tithe. Two houses, both glad about giving, each with its own shape for it.

how: Christians give through offerings, tithes and alms, and some churches read 2 Corinthians 9:7 as the offering is taken.

o: someone who gives gladly, by what they have
someone who gives the most money each week
someone who always smiles during church

games.q: a cheerful giver — tap the pairs.
p: accepted by what a man hath

s: Paul says God loves the biggest giver
God loveth a cheerful giver, and a gift is accepted according to what a person has.
the Macedonians gave out of deep poverty
the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality.
giving with a glad face is a teaching found only in Christianity
a hadith calls a smile in your brother's face charity: shared ground, in Islam's own words.

games.q: your youth group is raising money for a family whose house flooded. one kid has a few dollars and is embarrassed to give so little. what does Paul say?
o: it's accepted by what he has, not by what he hasn't.
he should wait until he can give as much as the others.
a gift only counts if it hurts, so he should borrow more.
games.why: if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.

practice: Let your face soften into a small smile, even alone in the room, and notice what it does to your shoulders and your breath.
Bring to mind one person you'll see today, and one small thing you could give them: time, a hand, a greeting. Keep the smile while you picture handing it over.

wordCard.voice: A cheerful giver. Paul's picture of giving from a willing heart, by what you have, not grudgingly.

carryVoice: The line to keep: a cheerful giver, glad to give by what you have, however small. See you soon.
